paras: The threatened lynching of Fortune Ellis took place in Lowndes County, Alabama, in October 1903, when a sheriff-led posse hunted Ellis, a Black man accused of shooting two white men in a dispute over cotton, while newspapers predicted he would be lynched. Ellis was captured and moved to the Montgomery County jail for fear of a mob, and no lynching was reported. The case drew a Birmingham Age-Herald editorial against 'a second lynching' that year, and in 1904 Ellis was fined $500 and given six months' hard labor.

J. B. Mitchell Jr. kept a store near Corrie with his father, a member of the county board of revenue. According to the first Letohatchie dispatch, Mitchell and his clerk, Will Davis, rode out on October 23 to see Ellis about five bales of cotton he was 'said to have stolen.' Ellis later said the cotton was his own picking, less than a bale, stored behind his house on the Brewer plantation, and that he refused to take it to the Mitchell gin because Mitchell had threatened his life.

The first reports said that as the two men approached, a Black man came to the door and fired buckshot into each of them at close range, and both were reported mortally wounded. The shooter was variously given as 'Fortune Ellis, or one of his sons,' Ellis and two sons, 'three negroes' and 'an unknown negro.' That night the sheriff and bloodhounds led a pursuit, and the Associated Press reported two Black men surrounded by 'a large posse.' The Letohatchie dispatch ended: 'The negroes will be lynched if captured.'
Ellis was taken in a church on the Brewer plantation. By his account, the white men fired on his house first, a bullet struck his head, not seriously, and he then fired his shotgun in self-defense.

Because the Lowndes jail was 'remotely situated,' a deputy sheriff took Ellis to Montgomery for safekeeping, for fear a mob would form to lynch him. On October 27 a second Black man, Shep Harris, was jailed there on a warrant for assault to murder; he denied any part beyond being at the scene. In August 1904, after 'a hard fought legal battle' in the Lowndes circuit court, Ellis was fined $500 with six months' hard labor added, for filling Mitchell with '550 shot' and shooting out Davis's eye. No death of either man, and no outcome for Harris or Ellis's sons, appears in the coverage.

All the coverage found came from white newspapers; no Black-press report was found. The Montgomery Advertiser's headline 'BUCKSHOT USEDBYBLACKS,' with the deck 'Murderers Pursued and Surrounded,' gave the white men's version without attribution and reported the expected lynching without comment. The Age-Herald ran the dispatch as 'Young Men Shot Down by Negroes,' adding that 'a Lynching is Feared.' A shorter Associated Press version ran in Savannah, Indianapolis and Raleigh papers, the last under the headline 'Surrounded by Avengers.'

On October 25 an Age-Herald editorial, 'Quick Trials for Lynchings,' urged the circuit judge to call a special term at once, saying it could try the accused 'in an hour's time.' It called the Black men who had the cotton 'anarchistic at the outset' and said their pursuers were now 'filled with the demoralizing spirit.' The Advertiser later printed Ellis's self-defense account beside the report of his removal.

The first dispatches said a Black man fired on the approaching white men, while Ellis said they fired on his house first; the 1904 court reports do not say who fired first. The cotton was stolen bales in the first reports but Ellis's own picking in his account.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Fortune Ellis
bases: A Black man accused of shooting two white men was hunted by a sheriff-led posse with bloodhounds while papers predicted he would be lynched if captured, and he was moved to another county's jail for fear of a mob (A1, A2, A8); no lynching took place.

No one was killed: Ellis was captured, jailed in Montgomery for safekeeping and sentenced in court in 1904 (A8, A12, A13); the large posse and the predicted lynching show only a threatened lynching (A1, A4).

The local Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the AP wire agree on the shooting, the pursuit and the lynching fear (A1, A3, A4), and the Advertiser and Age-Herald independently report the 1904 sentence (A12, A13); who fired first is contested by Ellis's own account (A8).

accounts.label: Associated Press
accounts.gist: The two men were shot by 'an unknown negro' over cotton said to have been stolen; two Black men were surrounded by a large posse.

accounts.label: Fortune Ellis's account
accounts.gist: The cotton was his own picking, less than a bale; he refused to take it to Mitchell's gin because Mitchell had threatened his life; the white men fired on his house first, wounding him, and he fired back in self-defense.

accounts.label: Circuit court report
accounts.gist: After a hard-fought trial Ellis was fined $500 and given six months' hard labor for shooting Mitchell and Davis.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser's first report, 'BUCKSHOT USEDBYBLACKS ... Murderers Pursued and Surrounded,' gave the white men's version as fact and stated without comment that the men would be lynched if captured; its later story printed Ellis's self-defense account.
The Birmingham Age-Herald's news headline 'Young Men Shot Down by Negroes' carried the deck 'a Lynching is Feared.'

The Age-Herald editorial 'Quick Trials for Lynchings' opposed a lynching, urging a special term that could try the accused 'in an hour's time,' while calling the Black men 'anarchistic at the outset.'
AP copy in Savannah, Indianapolis and Raleigh papers under headlines such as 'Surrounded by Avengers.'
